title: Store secrets in SSM Parameter Store
content:
Every SecureString under the path /student-market/dev/api becomes a configuration key of the API (the / separators map to :).
Parameter name Configuration key Value /student-market/dev/api/ConnectionStrings/DefaultConnection ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection Supabase transaction pooler string (port 6543, No Reset On Close=true) /student-market/dev/api/Jwt/SecretKey Jwt:SecretKey Random string, at least 32 characters /student-market/dev/api/OriginVerify/Secret OriginVerify:Secret Random string shared with CloudFront (step 5.5) /student-market/dev/api/Email/Password Email:Password Optional Gmail App Password for OTP emails Create the parameters function New-Secret { -join ((48..57 + 65..90 + 97..122) | Get-Random -Count 48 | ForEach-Object { [char]$_ }) } $path = "/student-market/dev/api" aws ssm put-parameter --name "$path/ConnectionStrings/DefaultConnection" --type SecureString ` --value "<transaction pooler connection string>" --overwrite --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 aws ssm put-parameter --name "$path/Jwt/SecretKey" --type SecureString --value (New-Secret) --overwrite --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 $originSecret = New-Secret aws ssm put-parameter --name "$path/OriginVerify/Secret" --type SecureString --value $originSecret --overwrite --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 Keep $originSecret in this terminal session; it is passed to the media stack in step 5.5.
Verify without revealing values aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path $path --recursive --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 ` --query "Parameters[].{Name:Name,Type:Type}" --output table All entries must have type SecureString. Avoid --with-decryption unless a value really needs to be read.

title: Proposal
content:
Student Flea Market A Cloud-Native Secondhand Marketplace for Students 1. Executive Summary Student Flea Market (Student Market) is an online marketplace where university students can buy, sell, or exchange textbooks, study materials, electronic devices, dormitory supplies, and other pre-owned items. The project addresses a common problem: listings are often scattered across social networks and chat groups, making them difficult to search, compare, manage, and verify.
The solution combines a responsive Next.js frontend hosted on Vercel, an ASP.NET Core 8 backend running on AWS Lambda, and PostgreSQL on Supabase. The backend provides protected REST APIs, enforces business rules, and issues short-lived presigned requests that allow browsers to upload images directly to Amazon S3. An event-driven Lambda function converts uploaded images into optimized WebP variants, which are delivered through Amazon CloudFront. CloudFront, protected by AWS WAF, is also the single public entry point for the API, while secrets are stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store.
The platform covers registration and login (email/password with OTP verification and Google sign-in), category browsing, search and filtering, seller-owned listings, secure image processing, favorites, exchange requests, transactions, reviews, reports, moderation, and chat. Chat works over REST on Lambda; realtime chat via SignalR runs on an optional ECS Fargate stack that is enabled only for demos.
2. Problem Statement Current Problem Students commonly use social networks, messaging groups, or personal contacts to exchange pre-owned items. This approach has several limitations:
Posts quickly become buried and cannot be filtered through a consistent structure. Descriptions, item condition, prices, and contact details do not follow a common standard. Buyers find it difficult to compare products or determine whether an item is still available. Sellers do not have a dedicated workflow for managing listings and images. Identity verification, ownership control, moderation, and reporting are limited. Uploading large images through a traditional API increases application server load and bandwidth usage. Proposed Solution Student Flea Market provides a centralized platform where students can register, sign in, browse and filter products, manage listings, upload images securely, save favorites, send exchange requests, track transactions, chat with sellers, leave reviews, and report violations.
The platform follows a cloud-native, cost-aware design. Request-driven components use managed, consumption-based AWS services (Lambda, API Gateway, S3, CloudFront), while PostgreSQL provides transactional consistency for users, products, exchanges, transactions, conversations, reviews, and reports. Components that would consume most of the AWS credit (frontend hosting and the relational database) are placed on free tiers of Vercel and Supabase.
Benefits Students: find suitable products and save money more quickly within a familiar community. Sellers: use a clear workflow for publishing listings and managing images. Campus community: encourage the reuse of textbooks and equipment while reducing waste. Administrators: moderate listings, manage users, categories, and moderators, and handle reports. Development team: work with a modular system that can be tested using PostgreSQL and LocalStack before deployment to AWS. 3. Project Scope Core Scope Account registration, email OTP verification, JWT login with refresh tokens, Google sign-in, and password reset. Product categories and paginated listings. Search and filtering by category. Create, view, update, and delete listings, with ownership checks so that only the seller can modify a listing. Direct image uploads using presigned S3 POST requests and automatic conversion to optimized WebP variants. Favorites, exchange requests, transactions (with payment confirmation), reviews, and violation reports. Buyer–seller chat over REST, with optional realtime delivery through SignalR. Administrative interface: moderation, users, sellers, categories, and moderators. Health checks, structured logging, validation, and consistent error responses. A responsive interface supporting Vietnamese and English, plus policy pages. Extended Scope Online payment gateways, product recommendations, analytics, and migrating the database to Amazon RDS (if the course requires everything to run on AWS) are left for later phases.
4. Solution Architecture Account-level services: AWS CloudTrail (management events in all Regions), IAM Access Analyzer, AWS Budgets, and Cost Explorer. All AWS resources are defined with AWS SAM/CloudFormation in the ap-southeast-1 Region, except the WAF web ACL, which must be created in us-east-1.
API Request Flow The user opens the static Next.js application hosted on Vercel. The frontend calls the API through CloudFront (/api/*), where AWS WAF applies rate limiting and managed rules. CloudFront forwards the request to API Gateway with a secret X-Origin-Verify header; requests that call API Gateway directly are rejected with 403. API Gateway invokes the ASP.NET Core API as an on-demand Lambda function. At cold start the API loads its secrets from SSM Parameter Store; it then validates the request, verifies the JWT, checks ownership, and reads or writes PostgreSQL through Entity Framework Core and the Supabase transaction pooler. Logs and operational metrics are sent to CloudWatch; alarms notify the team by email through SNS. HTTP API is suitable because the application needs REST/JSON routing and JWT-bearing requests but not usage plans, API keys, or response transformation. On-demand Lambda fits irregular early-stage traffic and does not require an application server to run when there are no requests. Because API Gateway with Lambda cannot keep long-lived WebSocket connections, realtime SignalR chat runs on a separate, optional ECS Fargate task behind an Application Load Balancer that only accepts traffic from CloudFront.
Image Upload and Processing Flow An authenticated seller requests permission to upload an image for a listing. The API validates the seller, listing, MIME type, file size, and number of images. The API returns a short-lived presigned S3 POST policy with a fixed object key. The browser uploads the file directly to the raw/ prefix of the private S3 bucket. The S3 ObjectCreated event invokes the image-processing Lambda function. Lambda generates thumbnail.webp (480px) and large.webp (1600px) under the processed/ prefix. CloudFront reads only processed images through Origin Access Control and caches them near users. Failed events are sent to an encrypted SQS failure queue, and a CloudWatch alarm on queue depth notifies the team. 5. Technologies and AWS Services Component Technology or service Responsibility Web interface Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript Responsive marketplace interface UI and state Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, TanStack Query, Zustand UI, server state, and client state Frontend hosting Vercel (Hobby) Static hosting, HTTPS, and Git-based deployments Edge and CDN Amazon CloudFront with OAC Image delivery, /api/* and /hubs/* routing Web protection AWS WAF Per-IP rate limit on /api, IP reputation, common rule set, known bad inputs Public API Amazon API Gateway HTTP API HTTPS entry point, routing, CORS, and throttling Backend ASP.NET Core 8 on AWS Lambda Authentication, validation, marketplace logic, ownership, and presigning Relational data Supabase PostgreSQL (Free, Singapore) Users, products, transactions, messages, and reports Data access Entity Framework Core and Npgsql Migrations, constraints, and queries Media storage Amazon S3 Private, versioned, encrypted raw and processed images Media processing AWS Lambda with Magick.NET Image validation and WebP generation Secrets AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store + AWS KMS SecureString DB connection string, JWT key, SMTP password, origin-verify secret Failure handling Amazon SQS Destination for failed image-processing events Alerting Amazon SNS Email notifications from CloudWatch alarms Observability Amazon CloudWatch Logs, metrics, retention, and alarms Audit and access AWS CloudTrail, IAM, IAM Access Analyzer Audit trail, least-privilege roles, external-access findings Realtime chat (optional) Amazon ECS Fargate, Application Load Balancer SignalR hub /hubs/chat on one ARM64 task Container build (optional) AWS CodeBuild, Amazon ECR Build the linux/arm64 API image on AWS and store it Infrastructure as Code AWS SAM and CloudFormation Repeatable stacks: media pipeline, API, edge WAF, realtime, build Cost control AWS Budgets, Cost Explorer Track spending against the available credit Local AWS emulation LocalStack Low-cost testing of S3 and the image pipeline 6. Data Design The relational model includes ApplicationUser, Category, Item, ItemImage, Favorite, ExchangeRequest, Transaction, Payment, Conversation, Message, Review, Report, and VerificationCode. Indexes and constraints enforce uniqueness, non-negative prices, valid ratings, ownership relationships, and efficient queries. Images are stored in object storage; the database stores references instead of binary image data.
7. Security Design Separate the deployment identity from Lambda runtime roles in accordance with least privilege; each Lambda has its own role. Protect seller operations with JWTs; the backend obtains the user ID from the verified token. Store secrets only in SSM Parameter Store as SecureString (KMS); never in source control, templates, or appsettings. Expose the API only through CloudFront + WAF; the backend rejects /api calls without the correct X-Origin-Verify header. Keep S3 buckets private, encrypted, protected by Block Public Access, and configured with ACLs disabled. Restrict presigned uploads by expiration time, object key, content type, and file size. Allow CloudFront OAC to read only processed images. Allow the optional ALB to accept traffic only from the CloudFront prefix list with the origin-verify header. Restrict CORS to the required HTTPS frontend origins. Do not log passwords, tokens, secrets, or complete presigned URLs. Use CloudWatch alarms with SNS email to monitor API errors, Lambda failures, throttling, duration, and the failure queue. Record management events with CloudTrail and review findings from IAM Access Analyzer. Enforce administrative permissions in the backend rather than relying only on the UI. 8. Budget Estimation The project is a course project funded by $170 of AWS credit on the AWS Free account plan; an AWS Budget of $10/month tracks spending. Moving frontend hosting to Vercel and PostgreSQL to Supabase removes the largest fixed costs (Amplify and RDS).

Credits are temporary discounts, not a long-term operating budget; if the course requires everything on AWS, the database can move to Amazon RDS by changing only the connection string and VPC parameters.
10. Risks and Mitigations Risk Impact Mitigation Low user adoption High Pilot with a group of students and prioritize simple posting and search flows Fraudulent listings High Ownership rules, reports, moderation, account status, and audit logs Unauthorized access or API abuse High JWT, least-privilege IAM, WAF rate limiting, origin-verify header, and negative tests Leaked secrets High SSM SecureString, no secrets in code, rotation of the origin-verify secret Malicious image uploads High Presigned constraints, MIME/magic-byte checks, limits, re-encoding, and private raw storage Duplicate or failed events Medium Idempotent object keys, deterministic output paths, retries, alarms, and SQS Unexpected costs Medium Budgets, alarms, lifecycle rules, log retention, and turning off the realtime stack Database interruption (Supabase Free pauses after 7 idle days, no restorable backups) High Restore before demos, scheduled access, and regular pg_dump backups Runtime end of support (dotnet8) Medium Plan migration to the dotnet10 Lambda runtime Excessive scope expansion Medium Separate core features from future features and define acceptance criteria 11. Next.js frontend on Vercel with authentication, Google sign-in, product search, listing management, chat, policy pages, and an administrative interface; ASP.NET Core 8 solution separating API, Application, Domain, Infrastructure, ImageProcessor, and Tests, running on Lambda behind API Gateway; PostgreSQL on Supabase with EF Core migrations and the full marketplace domain model; presigned S3 uploads and the S3-triggered .NET image processor with CloudFront delivery; CloudFront as the API entry point protected by AWS WAF; secrets in SSM Parameter Store; CloudTrail and IAM Access Analyzer enabled; optional realtime chat stack (ALB + ECS Fargate, image built by CodeBuild into ECR); SAM/CloudFormation templates, LocalStack setup, automated backend tests, and frontend lint/typecheck/static export. 12. Expected Outcomes A usable marketplace for the student community. Secure authentication and listing-management workflows. Direct uploads and optimized image delivery. title: Media pipeline: S3, Lambda, and CloudFront
content:
The media stack is deployed first because the API stack imports its outputs (bucket name, CloudFront URL, SNS topic).
How the pipeline works The API checks the seller and returns a short-lived presigned POST for a fixed key under raw/. ImageProcessor writes large.webp (1600px) and thumbnail.webp (480px) under processed/. CloudFront reads only processed/* through Origin Access Control; raw/ stays private and expires after 7 days. After two failed retries, the event is sent to an encrypted SQS failure queue. Contents Deploy the media stack Test the image pipeline

title: Serverless API: SSM, Lambda, and API Gateway
content:
The whole ASP.NET Core API runs as one Lambda function (AddAWSLambdaHosting(LambdaEventSource.HttpApi)) behind an API Gateway HTTP API. At cold start it loads its secrets from SSM Parameter Store, so the template contains no secret values.
Why this design HTTP API is enough: REST/JSON routing, CORS, and throttling (20 requests/s, burst 50), without API keys or usage plans. Lambda on demand costs nothing when there is no traffic. SSM SecureString keeps secrets encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/ssm; the Lambda role can only read its own path and decrypt through SSM. title: Edge security with AWS WAF
content:
So far the API is called directly on API Gateway. In this step CloudFront becomes the only public entry point: AWS WAF filters requests, CloudFront forwards /api/* to API Gateway with a secret X-Origin-Verify header, and the API rejects calls that do not carry it.
1. Create the WAF web ACL (us-east-1) WAF web ACLs for CloudFront must be created in us-east-1.
aws cloudformation deploy --template-file .\aws\iac\edge-waf.yaml ` --stack-name student-market-dev-edge --profile student-market --region us-east-1 ` --parameter-overrides Environment=dev SubscribeFreePlan=false IncludeSqliRule=false ApiRateLimitPer5Min=500 $webAcl = (aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name student-market-dev-edge --profile student-market --region us-east-1 ` --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='WebAclArn'].OutputValue" --output text) The web ACL has four rules: a per-IP rate limit of 500 /api requests per 5 minutes, the Amazon IP reputation list, the common rule set, and known bad inputs.
SubscribeFreePlan=false keeps usage-based WAF pricing (about $9/month for four rules). The CloudFront flat-rate Free plan cannot be subscribed from an account on the AWS Free account plan.
2. Attach WAF and route /api/* through CloudFront Redeploy the media stack with the web ACL, the API domain, and the origin secret from step 5.4.1:
$apiDomain = "<ApiOriginDomain>" sam deploy --template-file .\.aws-sam\build-media-pipeline\template.yaml ` --stack-name student-market-dev-media ` --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM --resolve-s3 --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 ` --parameter-overrides Environment=dev EnableAuditLogging=true AlertEmail=<alert-email> "FrontendOrigins=http://localhost:3000" ` WebAclArn=$webAcl ApiOriginDomain=$apiDomain OriginVerifySecret=$originSecret 3. Enforce origin verification on the API sam deploy --template-file .\.aws-sam\build-api\template.yaml ` --stack-name student-market-dev ` --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM --resolve-s3 --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 ` --parameter-overrides Environment=dev MediaStackName=student-market-dev-media ` SsmParameterPath=/student-market/dev/api SkipDatabaseSeed=true EnforceOriginVerify=true ` "FrontendOrigins=http://localhost:3000" 4. Test $cdn = "<CloudFrontBaseUrl>"; $api = "<ApiBaseUrl>" curl.exe -s -o NUL -w "%{http_code}`n" "$cdn/api/Items/search" # 200 through CloudFront curl.exe -s -o NUL -w "%{http_code}`n" "$api/api/Items/search" # 403 ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED curl.exe -s -o NUL -w "%{http_code}`n" "$cdn/api/Items/search?q=%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C%2Fscript%3E" # XSS payload blocked by WAF (403) Finally point the frontend to CloudFront (NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=<CloudFrontBaseUrl>/api) and, once the real HTTPS frontend domain is available, redeploy both stacks with FrontendOrigins=<that domain>.

Empty the media bucket and delete the media stack Use the S3 console: select the bucket → Empty → type permanently delete. Do the same for the CloudTrail/audit log bucket if the stack created one. Then:
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name student-market-dev-media --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name student-market-dev-media --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 Deleting the CloudFront distribution takes several minutes because it must be disabled first.
3. Delete the WAF stack (us-east-1) aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name student-market-dev-edge --profile student-market --region us-east-1 4. Delete the SSM parameters aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /student-market/dev/api --recursive --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 ` --query "Parameters[].Name" --output text | ForEach-Object { $_ -split "\s+" } | Where-Object { $_ } | ForEach-Object { aws ssm delete-parameter --name $_ --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 } 5. Final checks aws cloudformation list-stacks --stack-status-filter CREATE_COMPLETE UPDATE_COMPLETE --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 ` --query "StackSummaries[?starts_with(StackName,'student-market')].StackName" aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda/student-market --profile student-market --region ap-southeast-1 ` --query "logGroups[].logGroupName" Delete any leftover log groups, and remove the SAM artifact stack aws-sam-cli-managed-default if SAM is no longer used. The Supabase database and the Vercel project are outside AWS and are not affected.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Below are my personal reflections on my experience in the First Cloud AI Journey program, shared to help the FCAJ team improve the program for future cohorts.
Overall Evaluation 1. Working Environment
The environment is friendly and open, and people are always willing to help when I run into difficulties. The 12-week learning path is clearly structured — from cloud fundamentals, IAM, compute, storage, and networking to serverless, IaC, monitoring, and security — so I always knew what to focus on each week.
2. Support from Mentor / Team Admin
The mentor explains clearly and encourages me to research and try things myself before asking. This approach helped me solve many problems on my own while building Student Market, such as choosing Supabase instead of RDS to save credit, or moving realtime chat to ECS Fargate after discovering that SignalR cannot run on API Gateway + Lambda. The admin team handled program procedures and documents well.
3. Relevance of Work to Academic Major
My major is Artificial Intelligence, so most of the cloud, infrastructure, and security knowledge was new to me. Still, my programming background from university helped me catch up, and cloud knowledge is an essential foundation for deploying AI applications in the future.
4. Learning & Skill Development Opportunities
This is the part I value most. Through Student Market, I went through a complete cycle: designing the architecture, writing IaC with AWS SAM, deploying to production, configuring WAF, SSM Parameter Store, CloudWatch alarms, and CloudTrail, and tracking costs with AWS Budgets. Beyond technical skills, I also learned to write worklogs and deployment documentation and to collaborate with teammates through Git.
5. Company Culture & Team Spirit
Everyone respects each other and works seriously while keeping things relaxed. Teammates are willing to share knowledge and debug problems together.
6. Internship Policies / Benefits
Receiving $170 of AWS credit to practice on a real account is a big plus; it taught me how to operate a real system instead of only reading theory. The program’s events and workshops also kept me up to date with new knowledge.
Additional Questions What did you find most satisfying during your internship?
Taking a real project all the way to production on AWS myself — from design to security and monitoring — and understanding why each service was chosen. What do you think the company should improve for future interns?
Provide early guidance on the limits of the AWS Free account plan (for example, the CloudFront Free plan cannot be subscribed, so WAF must be paid) and on how to request IAM permissions, since our team lost time waiting for permissions before we could deploy. If recommending to a friend, would you suggest they intern here? Why or why not?
Yes. The program has a clear learning path, credit to practice on real AWS, and a capstone project large enough to apply almost everything learned. Suggestions & Expectations Add a session on cost management and resource cleanup (Budgets, tagging, teardown) in the first weeks, so interns avoid spending credit unexpectedly. Hold mid-term architecture reviews with mentors to catch unsuitable choices early (such as WebSockets on Lambda) before deployment. Share more templates or reference examples for IaC, CI/CD, and security (WAF, secrets, least privilege) so teams have a common starting point. I would like to continue with future FCAJ programs, especially AI/ML on AWS, to combine with my major.

title: Week 12 Worklog
content:
Week 12 — Capstone: Student Market Timeline: 24/11/2026 – 29/11/2026
Weekly objective Consolidate the course by analyzing, explaining, and reviewing the AWS architecture of Student Market — a second-hand marketplace for students (textbooks, study materials, used items) with a Next.js frontend and an ASP.NET Core (.NET 8) REST API.
Learning plan Session Date Topic 1 Tue, 24/11/2026 Define functional and non-functional requirements; map each component to where it runs (AWS, Vercel, Supabase) and why. 2 Wed, 25/11/2026 API flow: Client → CloudFront (AWS WAF) → API Gateway HTTP API → Lambda (.NET 8) → PostgreSQL; secrets from SSM Parameter Store (SecureString/KMS). 3 Thu, 26/11/2026 Media pipeline: presigned upload to private S3 raw/ → S3 event → ImageProcessor Lambda (WebP) → processed/ → CloudFront with OAC; failures to SQS. 4 Fri, 27/11/2026 Security and operations: least-privilege IAM roles, WAF rules, CloudWatch alarms → SNS, CloudTrail, IAM Access Analyzer; optional realtime chat on ECS Fargate + ALB with images built by CodeBuild into ECR. 5 Sun, 29/11/2026 IaC with AWS SAM/CloudFormation (4 stacks), cost review with Budgets/Cost Explorer, cleanup plan; complete diagrams, ADRs, and review questions. AWS services used by Student Market Group Service Role in Student Market Compute AWS Lambda API Lambda runs the whole ASP.NET Core backend (auth/JWT, listings, categories, REST chat, presigned upload links); ImageProcessor Lambda creates large.webp (1600px) and thumbnail.webp (480px). API Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Public HTTPS entry for the API, with CORS for the frontend origin. Storage Amazon S3 Private, versioned, encrypted media bucket: raw/ for original uploads, processed/ for WebP images. Delivery Amazon CloudFront CDN for processed/ images through Origin Access Control; also routes /api/* to API Gateway with an X-Origin-Verify header. Security AWS WAF Web ACL on CloudFront: per-IP /api rate limit, IP reputation, common rule set, known bad inputs. Security AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store + AWS KMS SecureString secrets (DB connection string, JWT key, SMTP password, origin-verify secret) loaded at cold start. Security AWS IAM, IAM Access Analyzer One least-privilege role per Lambda, a deployer user/policy, and an account analyzer for external access. Messaging Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS SQS failure queue for image processing; SNS topic sending alarm emails. Observability Amazon CloudWatch Structured logs with retention and alarms for errors, throttles, duration, and queue depth. Audit AWS CloudTrail Management events in all Regions, logged to a dedicated S3 bucket. Realtime (optional) Amazon ECS (Fargate), Elastic Load Balancing (ALB) One ARM64 task serving the SignalR hub /hubs/chat; the ALB only accepts traffic from CloudFront. Enabled only for demos (~$1.3/day). Build (optional) AWS CodeBuild, Amazon ECR Build the linux/arm64 API image on AWS and store it in ECR. IaC AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM Stacks media-pipeline, api, edge-waf (us-east-1), realtime + build. Cost AWS Budgets, Cost Explorer Track spending against the $170 credit. Status: Student Market is deployed to production — the API, media pipeline, and WAF run on AWS, and the frontend is live on Vercel. The realtime stack is enabled only for demos.
Outside AWS: the frontend is hosted on Vercel (Hobby) and PostgreSQL runs on Supabase (Free, Singapore, through the transaction pooler). Because of that, the project does not use RDS, VPC/NAT Gateway, EC2, Cognito, or Amplify.
Setup to understand Read the project’s SAM templates and the deployment order: database → media pipeline → API → WAF (us-east-1) → frontend → update CORS with the real domain. Main Region is ap-southeast-1. Use sam validate --lint and LocalStack to check things locally before touching a real account.
Reference model Users (browser) | | HTTPS +------------+--------------+ v v Vercel (Next.js) Amazon CloudFront <-- AWS WAF | | /api/* | | processed/* (OAC) v v API Gateway HTTP API S3 media bucket (private) | raw/ processed/ v | ^ Lambda API (.NET 8) | ObjectCreated| write WebP | | | v | SSM Parameter | | | Lambda ImageProcessor+ Store (KMS) <-+ | | | | | +--> SQS (failures) presigned URL -+ v Supabase PostgreSQL (pooler :6543) CloudWatch logs/alarms --> SNS (email) CloudTrail + IAM Access Analyzer Optional: CloudFront /hubs/* --> ALB --> ECS Fargate (SignalR), image from CodeBuild -> ECR Learning outcomes Completed the Student Market architecture diagram and data-flow explanation (API flow and image upload flow). Prepared a table describing every AWS service and why it was selected over alternatives (Lambda vs. EC2/Fargate, Supabase vs. RDS, Vercel vs. Amplify). Analyzed risks: leaked secrets, public bucket exposure, API abuse, image-processing failures, Supabase pausing after 7 idle days, and cost of the realtime stack. Wrote a final reflection and next-learning plan. Self-review questions Why does the browser upload directly to S3 with a presigned URL instead of sending the image through the API? How do OAC and the bucket policy ensure only processed/* is publicly readable through CloudFront? Why must the Lambda API use the Supabase pooler (port 6543) instead of a direct connection? Why are secrets stored in SSM Parameter Store instead of CloudFormation parameters or appsettings? If ImageProcessor fails, how does the system observe it (CloudWatch alarm, SQS queue, SNS email) and recover?
